stories.title: OpenAI claims the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4
stories.plain: OpenAI published a manuscript claiming a matching lower bound for matrix multiplication, which would make the best possible exponent exactly 9/4 rather than merely at most 9/4. It comes with a formal Lean statement of the exponent, but no independent audit and no peer review.
stories.eng: In October an unreleased OpenAI model produced a proof that omega, the matrix multiplication exponent, is at most 9/4, avoiding the laser method behind every record since the 1980s and reducing the problem to how fast polynomials can be multiplied. The 24 November manuscript claims a matching lower bound over every field, closing the gap. OpenAI released a formal Lean statement of the exact exponent, but the finite-size nonscalar-gate lower bound is still unformalised.
stories.point: The point: an AI-produced line of work is now claiming to close a 50-year-old open question, not just nudge it, and the Lean artefacts decide how much of that claim anyone can check.
stories.means: Multiplying two n-by-n matrices the schoolbook way costs about n^3 operations, and omega is the smallest exponent achievable in principle. For decades records moved in the fourth decimal place, from about 2.3729 to 2.371177 this August. The October AI result pushed the ceiling to 2.25, and this new claim says nothing can ever beat 2.25 either, which would settle the value. These are asymptotic statements with enormous hidden constants, and OpenAI's own paper says the construction gives no competitive matrix size, so no real kernel gets faster.
stories.industry: Labs are competing to show models producing original mathematics, and after this month's Riemann Hypothesis and VP vs VNP claims, shipping Lean artefacts has become the expected standard. The weak point is always whatever was left unformalised, which here is part of the new lower bound.
stories.you: Do not expect faster matmuls in your framework from this. The transferable habit is to ask, of any AI-generated result, which parts are machine-checked and which are prose, then review the prose parts first.
terms: Matrix multiplication exponent
The smallest power k such that n-by-n matrices can be multiplied in roughly n^k arithmetic operations.
Lower bound
A proof that no algorithm can do better than a stated cost.
Lean
A proof assistant that checks every step of a formal proof by computer.
stories.why: Kingy AI's breakthrough tracker marks the claim provisional and found no completed independent audit of the lower bound.
stories.source: OpenAI preprint via Kingy AI tracker · 25 Nov; The Neuron · 25 Nov

stories.title: OpenAI says GPT-6 designs proteins with reasoning and code alone
stories.plain: OpenAI published lab results in which proteins designed by its GPT-6 models stuck to five chosen targets. The models wrote the designs using general reasoning and code, without calling any specialised biology model for the design step.
stories.eng: Backbones came from a pre-release GPT-6.2; SolubleMPNN supplied sequences and Boltz-2, OpenDDE and ESMFold2 filtered candidates before synthesis at partner lab Onava. Of 322 minibinders tested against PD-L1, IL-7Ra, TrkA, VEGF-A and IL-17A, 35 bound (10.9%), with per-target hits of 5, 3, 1, 8 and 18. On antibody work, 128 of 182 redesigned VHH loops against IL-4Ra bound, and full structure prediction remains weak: mean TM-score 0.38 for the internal model against 0.93 for ESMFold2.
stories.point: The point: a general text-and-code model, with no protein-specific architecture, now gets non-trivial hit rates in a wet lab, which blurs the line between general models and scientific tools.
stories.means: Protein design has been the domain of specialised systems like RFdiffusion that generate 3D structures directly. The claim here is that a general model can reason its way to a design and write the code to express it, reaching comparable computational scores and real binding in vitro. A 10.9% hit rate means most designs fail, which is normal in this field, and binding is only the first requirement: specificity, stability, potency and safety all come later. OpenAI says the results do not yet establish end-to-end zero-shot design, since specialised tools still did the sequence and filtering steps.
stories.industry: This is the strongest recent evidence for the general-models-eat-vertical-tools thesis, and it lands alongside Anthropic's own protein binder run and Novartis's CEO saying AI could cut four years from drug development. It also sharpens biosecurity arguments, which OpenAI addresses through its Preparedness Framework.
stories.you: The pattern worth copying is the pipeline, not the hype: a general model proposes, specialised models filter, and a lab provides ground truth. If you build in a technical domain, the question is which of your specialised components a general model can now replace at the proposal stage.
terms: Minibinder
A small designed protein meant to stick to a chosen target protein.
TM-score
A 0-to-1 measure of how closely a predicted protein structure matches the real one.
RFdiffusion
A specialised generative model for designing protein structures.
stories.why: Self-reported in a preprint that has not been peer reviewed; reported hit rates depend on filtering strictness and the definition of binding.
stories.source: OpenAI · 24 Nov; Let's Data Science · 24 Nov

stories.title: NHS starts AI breast screening trial with nearly 700,000 women
stories.plain: The NHS is testing AI-assisted breast cancer screening across a trial involving close to 700,000 women. The aim is to see whether AI raises detection rates and reduces the reading workload on radiologists.
stories.eng: Screening mammograms in the UK are normally double-read by two radiologists; the trial tests whether an AI reader can take one of those slots or triage cases before human review. The design compares detection rates and workload against standard double reading at national screening scale.
specs: higher detection rate, lower radiologist workload
stories.point: The point: this is AI imaging being tested as a policy change at national scale, where the outcome measure is cancers found, not benchmark accuracy.
stories.means: Breast screening in the UK uses two independent radiologists per scan, which is reliable but consumes scarce specialist time. AI models have matched radiologists on retrospective datasets for years, but that says little about live screening, where prevalence is low and false positives mean real recalls and biopsies. A trial at this size can measure whether AI finds cancers earlier and how many extra recalls it generates. It also arrives as vision-language models begin drafting radiology reports, discussed at the RSNA meeting this month.
stories.industry: Health systems are the hardest customers for AI, with the longest validation cycles and the clearest accountability, so a national trial carries more weight than vendor benchmarks. If it works, the pattern of AI replacing one of two human readers is directly reusable in other double-read workflows.
stories.you: If you build AI for regulated domains, note the evaluation shape: live deployment against the existing human process, measured on the outcome people care about rather than on a held-out test set.
terms: Double reading
Two radiologists independently reading the same scan to reduce missed cancers.
Triage
Sorting cases by likely urgency so humans look at the riskiest first.
stories.why: Trial results are not yet available; the screening programme is still running on standard double reading.

stories.title: MCP servers can now ship skills, and Tasks reaches general release
stories.plain: Anthropic put Skills over MCP into public beta, so a connected server can supply instructions as well as tools. Tasks and Elicitation, which let a server run long jobs and pause to ask the user something, are now generally available.
stories.eng: A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md plus optional files, served through MCP Resources: the client discovers which skills a server offers at connect time and loads the full instructions only when needed. Tasks lets a server run a long operation or a full agent loop while the model continues and collects the result later; Elicitation pauses a tool call to request input through a form or link. The spec labels server-supplied skills a prompt injection risk and requires explicit per-skill approval before local code execution, with re-approval when a skill's files change.
specs: public beta, on by default for Pro, Max, Ultra
stories.point: The point: connecting a server now imports behaviour, not just capability, which changes what an organisation is actually approving.
stories.means: MCP started two years ago as a way to give models tools: a server exposed functions and the model called them. Skills invert part of that, letting the server also ship the procedure for using them, so a merchant platform can supply the whole workflow for updating a store rather than 40 loose endpoints. That saves context, because instructions load only when relevant, and it keeps the procedure updated with the server. It also means text you did not write enters the model's instructions, which is why the spec demands per-skill approval and re-approval on change.
stories.industry: This is the integration layer consolidating: tool search, tasks, elicitation and now skills all push coordination work out of the agent framework and into the protocol. Microsoft added skills over MCP in VS Code 1.147, so this is becoming a cross-client standard rather than one vendor's feature.
stories.you: Review server-supplied skills the way you review a dependency, because they are instructions with your credentials attached. Note that Claude Code ignores some settings a skill declares, including tool-permission and hook settings, so do not rely on a skill to constrain itself.
terms: MCP
Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting models to external tools and data.
Skill
A folder with a SKILL.md file of instructions that a model loads when a task calls for it.
Elicitation
A server pausing mid-call to ask the user for input, then continuing.
stories.why: The extension spec is beta and client and SDK support is still being built.

stories.title: Unit 42: autonomous agents ran over 10 intrusion campaigns
stories.plain: Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 reported that attackers used autonomous AI agents in more than 10 campaigns worldwide between July and September. The agents worked so fast that intrusions took hours instead of weeks, but their behaviour gave them away as non-human.
stories.eng: Initial access came through web shells planted via vulnerable web applications; the agents then ran hundreds of unique commands within minutes. Unit 42 says the machine-speed operation traded stealth for throughput, and that behavioural fingerprints such as visible reasoning steps identified non-human operators. Targeted sectors were government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture and education.
specs: hundreds of unique commands in minutes
government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture, education
stories.point: The point: agent-run intrusions are now a measured category rather than a demo, and their biggest tell is the speed and shape of their activity, not the exploits they use.
stories.means: A human intruder spends days on reconnaissance and lateral movement, which is what most detection is tuned to. An agent compresses that into minutes, which breaks the assumption that defenders have time to react but also makes the activity statistically obvious: nobody types hundreds of distinct commands in a few minutes. That is the trade Unit 42 describes, speed bought with stealth. The exploits themselves are ordinary, which means the defence is still patching exposed web applications.
stories.industry: This lands in the same week as Amazon's report on agentic frameworks stealing LLM API keys to fund further attacks, and the AWS CEO arguing that AI safety needs foundational engineering rather than an emergency brake. Agent security is becoming its own product category on both sides.
stories.you: If you own detection rules, rate-of-action signals are now worth more than they were: commands per minute, breadth of unique commands, and timing regularity. On the defensive basics, exposed web applications and web shells remain the entry point.
terms: Web shell
A script left on a web server that lets an attacker run commands on it.
Behavioural fingerprint
A pattern in how actions are performed that identifies the kind of operator behind them.
stories.why: Unit 42 reports campaign activity it observed; the agents' own reported outcomes cannot be independently verified.
stories.source: Unit 42 (Palo Alto Networks) via RIO Rundown · 25 Nov

stories.title: XPENG debuts IRON humanoid and a three-layer physical AI stack
stories.plain: XPENG showed its IRON humanoid robot and a new physical AI architecture at its AI Day. The robot is scheduled to start training as a shop assistant in XPENG stores in early 2027, with a public release targeted for the middle of that year.
stories.eng: The Turing Physical AI Architecture (VLA 3.0) has three layers: System 0 folds body control, power and actuation into the AI loop; System 1 is the real-time layer running VLA 2.0; System 2 does slow cognition, pairing vision-language task planning with an Agent Runtime state machine. VLA 2.0 version 6.4.0 adds agent-driven closed-loop training, which XPENG says raises training speed 10 to 12 times and enables self-distillation. IRON has 76 degrees of freedom, more than 1,500 tactile sensing points covering over 80% of key body areas, and three in-house Turing AI chips.
stories.point: The point: a carmaker is reusing its driving stack for a humanoid, and the tactile sensing count signals that the hard problem has moved from walking to touching things.
stories.means: Most humanoid demos are impressive at locomotion and poor at contact: picking things up, handing them over, not crushing them. More than 1,500 tactile points is a bet that dense touch sensing, not better vision, is what makes manipulation reliable. The three-layer split matters too, because folding body control into the AI loop (System 0) is how you stop the planner from asking for motions the body cannot execute. XPENG also reports its driving models in the same architecture: a 12.4% range gain in urban congestion from VLA adaptive deceleration, with an OTA in December.
stories.industry: The same vision-language-action recipe now spans cars, robotaxis and humanoids, which is why automakers are the best-capitalised humanoid builders. Deployment into a company's own retail stores first is the standard de-risking move, as with Ant Group's wheeled service humanoid earlier this week.
stories.you: If you work on robot software, the architectural idea to take away is the fast and slow split with a state machine between them: a language model plans, a real-time policy acts, and a deterministic runtime arbitrates. Expect tactile data pipelines to become as demanding as camera pipelines.
terms: VLA
Vision-language-action model: one model that takes images and instructions and outputs robot actions.
Degrees of freedom
The number of independently controllable joints or axes in a robot.
Self-distillation
Training a model on its own outputs to compress or stabilise what it has learned.
stories.why: All performance figures are XPENG's own, announced at its AI Day; none are independently tested.
stories.source: XPENG via GlobeNewswire · 25 Nov; CnEVPost · 25 Nov

stories.title: EU proposes a Quantum Act and a sovereign tech equity fund
stories.plain: The European Commission proposed a Quantum Act to turn EU quantum research into products, secure supply chains and prepare systems for post-quantum cryptography. It also set out a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund to put money into technologies it treats as strategically essential.
stories.eng: The Act has three pillars, research excellence, deployment and security, delivered through the Quantum Europe Framework Initiative. Deployment measures include Grand Challenges competitions, pan-European quantum computers, simulators and quantum-enhanced medical imaging, and innovation hubs for start-ups. On security, the Commission and member states would monitor supply chains, identify critical suppliers and components, and run a coordinated post-quantum cryptography transition with preparedness monitoring and procurement safeguards.
specs: over 11 billion euros, EU plus member states
Quantum Strategy Board, European Quantum Alliance
proposal, now goes to Parliament and Council
stories.point: The point: Europe is treating quantum the way it treated chips, as an industrial sovereignty problem with an equity fund attached rather than a research grant question.
stories.means: Europe funds strong quantum research and then watches the companies raise their growth money elsewhere, which is the gap an equity vehicle is meant to close. The security pillar is the part with near-term consequences for software: a coordinated post-quantum cryptography transition means public bodies will start requiring PQC-ready systems through procurement. The Act is a proposal, so the funding figures attached to it depend on later budget decisions, and the 11 billion euros cited is existing investment, not new money.
stories.industry: Quantum procurement is accelerating in parallel, with IQM selling a 54-qubit system into a Seoul data centre the same day and Korea planning over 200 trillion won of R&D to 2030. State money is becoming the main demand signal in this sector.
stories.you: The actionable piece is PQC. If you own anything that stores long-lived encrypted data or ships long-lived devices, inventory your cryptography now, because procurement rules will arrive before the hardware threat does.
terms: Post-quantum cryptography
Encryption designed to stay secure against future quantum computers.
Sovereign Tech Equity Fund
A proposed EU vehicle providing equity financing for technologies deemed strategically essential.
stories.why: The Quantum Act names no funding amount of its own; future money depends on EU budget decisions.
stories.source: European Commission · 25 Nov; The Quantum Insider · 25 Nov

stories.title: IQM to put a 54-qubit machine in a Seoul data centre next to GPUs
stories.plain: Finnish maker IQM received an order from Korean company QAI for a 54-qubit quantum computer to be installed in QAI's Seoul data centre. QAI plans to sell access to it alongside GPU infrastructure as a service.
stories.eng: The system is an IQM Radiance R3, designed for HPC integration, with high-fidelity gates and tunable couplers in a square lattice whose layout natively supports surface-code error correction. Customers own and operate it on site with pulse-level access and an option to upgrade chips and components. Delivery and installation are expected by the end of 2027, and IQM calls it the first of its systems in a private data centre in Asia.
stories.point: The point: quantum processors are being bought as data centre line items to sit beside GPUs, which is the hybrid model the field has been promising for years.
stories.means: A standalone quantum computer solves nothing useful today, because real workloads need classical compute for the bulk of the work and for error correction in the loop. Putting the machine in a commercial data centre next to GPUs is what makes that loop short enough to matter, and pulse-level access means customers can program the hardware directly rather than through a fixed gate set. Fifty-four qubits with surface-code-friendly layout is a research-scale machine, not a useful one, so the named use cases, drug discovery, battery materials, portfolio and logistics optimisation, are pipeline-building rather than production.
stories.industry: This is the same pattern as AMD taking a stake in PsiQuantum and tuning a real-time decoder for accelerators: the commercial unit is a quantum-plus-classical system, sold to clouds and national programmes. Korea's strategy, aiming at the world's highest quantum utilisation rate by 2035, is the demand behind it.
stories.you: Nothing to build on yet, but the interface worth watching is the scheduler: when quantum jobs queue next to GPU jobs, you get an ordinary resource allocation problem, and that is where software engineers will first touch this hardware.
terms: Tunable coupler
A controllable connection between two qubits, letting you switch their interaction on and off.
Surface code
A leading error-correction scheme that spreads one logical qubit across a grid of physical ones.
Pulse-level access
Programming the hardware's analogue control signals directly instead of using preset gates.
stories.why: No purchase price was disclosed; the machine is not due until the end of 2027.

stories.title: Tidal to delete fully AI-generated tracks and auto-reject new ones
stories.plain: Tidal said it will remove around 29 million wholly AI-generated songs on 9 December and automatically reject new uploads from generators such as Suno. Detection is imperfect, so some human-made tracks will be caught by mistake.
stories.eng: Tidal uses detection software from Ircam Amplify, which claims 99% accuracy at a 1% false-positive rate: at this scale that implies roughly 290,000 legitimate tracks could be misflagged, and Tidal has not described recourse for wrongly flagged artists. Its published AI policy acts only on recordings judged wholly AI-generated, citing detection limits and false-positive risk, labels them, excludes them from royalty attribution and lets listeners switch them off; it says it will extend action to substantially AI-generated recordings as detection improves.
specs: Ircam Amplify, claimed 99% accuracy, 1% false positives
Share of recent uploads wholly AI-generated
stories.point: The point: a platform is now willing to accept hundreds of thousands of false positives to keep generated content out, which is a precedent for every service drowning in model output.
stories.means: Streaming economics assume a roughly fixed supply of human recordings; generators broke that, and 43% of recent uploads being wholly AI-generated is the result. Tidal's policy is a classifier decision applied at catalogue scale, where even a 1% false-positive rate means a very large absolute number of wrongly removed works. The mitigating fact is that 96% of the identified AI tracks have no streams, so the fraud being targeted is royalty farming rather than listening. Note that the policy distinguishes wholly from partly AI-generated, and anything below that threshold stays unlabelled.
stories.industry: Platforms are converging on provenance and detection rather than outright bans on AI tools, which keeps AI-assisted music allowed while cutting off generated bulk. The same classifier-at-scale problem is appearing in app stores, review sites and open-source registries.
stories.you: This is a false-positive budgeting problem of exactly the kind you face when you deploy a classifier on millions of items. The lesson is that the appeals path, not the accuracy number, is what determines whether the deployment is defensible.
terms: False positive rate
The share of legitimate items a detector wrongly flags.
Royalty farming
Uploading large volumes of low-effort tracks to collect small streaming payouts.
stories.why: Tidal's own AI policy page describes labelling, royalty exclusion and removal of wholly AI-generated recordings, and does not publish track counts.
stories.source: Pitchfork via RIO Rundown · 25 Nov; TechCrunch · 24 Nov; Tidal AI policy

stories.title: California law sets rules for AI use by lawyers and arbitrators
stories.plain: California enacted SB 574, which requires attorneys and arbitrators to verify AI output and disclose AI assistance in court filings. It also bans handing legal practice or decision-making authority to an AI system.
stories.eng: The statute puts verification and disclosure duties on legal professionals rather than on the model vendor, and prohibits delegating the practice of law or adjudicative decision-making to generative AI. Arbitrators specifically cannot delegate decision-making authority. It takes effect on 1 January 2027.
specs: verify AI output, disclose AI assistance in filings
delegating legal practice or decision-making to AI
stories.point: The point: regulation of professional AI use is arriving as duties on the human in the chair, not as restrictions on the model.
stories.means: Courts have spent two years sanctioning lawyers for citing cases that models invented, handled case by case under existing rules of conduct. A statute changes that into a standing obligation with a disclosure requirement, so the question in a filing becomes what was checked, not whether AI was used. The ban on delegating decision-making is aimed at arbitration, where a private decision-maker could quietly let a model decide an outcome. Because the duty sits with the professional, the practical effect is demand for audit trails showing what the model produced and what a human verified.
stories.industry: This is the shape of near-term AI rules in regulated professions: disclosure and human accountability instead of model licensing, matching the UK FCA setting out expectations for firms deploying agentic AI the same week. Legal tech vendors will be judged on provenance and citation checking.
stories.you: If you build tools for regulated users, logging becomes a feature: which model, which prompt, which output, and which human approved it. Verification UI is now a compliance requirement in California, not a nice extra.
terms: Generative AI
Models that produce new text, images or code rather than classifying existing data.
Arbitrator
A private decision-maker who resolves a dispute outside the courts.
stories.why: The law applies to California attorneys and arbitrators and takes effect at the start of 2027.

concepts.desc: Robots moving from demos into shops, pharmacies, warehouses and public markets.

XPENG debuts IRON, 76 degrees of freedom and 1,500+ tactile points, to train as a store assistant in its own shops in Q1 2027.
23 Nov
Ant Group leads a $100M round at $1.6B for Simplexity's iX wheeled service humanoid; Unitree shares hit their 20% limit on a Chinese elder-care robot plan.
22 Nov
Nvidia unveils Agile ONE SN reference humanoid (31 DoF, early 2027), open-source Isaac OS and Isaac Lab 3.0 GA at GTC Berlin.
17 Nov
Genesis AI raises $500M; it has built 30 to 40 Eno humanoids trained on sensor-glove data and is piloting with a few customers, but its hands last only weeks.
16 Nov
GXO and Apptronik plan up to 1,000 Apollo humanoids over four years under RaaS, gated on KPIs, first deployment late 2027.
13 Nov
OpenAI folds its robotics team into core research, says GPT-6 Astra can control robots directly, and targets a humanoid demo in 2027.

eras.name: Large language models
eras.short: Models trained to predict the next word turn out to write, translate and code.
eras.how: A transformer is trained on a large share of the public internet to predict the next token. Capabilities appear with scale: GPT-3 could do tasks it was never trained for, given a few examples in the prompt.
eras.built: Autocomplete, text generation APIs, early GitHub Copilot.
eras.broke: Raw models ramble, make things up and do not follow instructions reliably.

eras.name: Chatbots
eras.short: Instruction tuning and human feedback make models useful in a conversation.
eras.how: Fine-tune the base model on examples of good answers, then use reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) so it prefers helpful, safe replies.
eras.built: Chat interfaces, customer support bots, writing assistants.
eras.broke: The model only knows its training data and cannot look anything up or do anything.

eras.name: RAG and tool use
eras.short: Models get access to your documents and to APIs.
eras.how: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt. Function calling lets the model output a structured call to an API you define.
eras.broke: One question, one answer. Multi-step tasks still needed a human driving every step.

eras.name: Workflows
eras.short: Engineers chain model calls into fixed pipelines.
eras.how: You write the steps in code: classify, then retrieve, then draft, then check. The model fills in each step, but the control flow is yours.
eras.built: Document processing pipelines, LangChain-style chains, eval harnesses.
eras.broke: Fixed pipelines break on anything you did not anticipate. Real tasks need the system to decide what to do next.

eras.name: Agents
eras.short: The model decides the next step itself, in a loop with tools.
eras.how: A loop: the model looks at the goal and results so far, picks a tool, runs it, reads the output, repeats until done. Reasoning models that think before answering made these loops far more reliable.
eras.built: Coding agents, computer-use agents, MCP servers that expose tools to any agent.
eras.broke: Agents worked for minutes, then drifted, looped or lost track on long tasks.

eras.name: Autonomous agents
eras.short: Agents run for hours on real work in sandboxes, with little supervision.
eras.how: Better long-horizon training, sandboxed environments, checkpoints and the ability to run tests let an agent own a whole task: open the repo, make the change, run CI, open a pull request.
eras.built: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity; agents opening PRs while you sleep.
eras.broke: One agent is one thread of work. Large problems need many in parallel.

eras.name: Multi-agent orchestration
eras.short: A planner agent splits work across specialist agents.
eras.how: An orchestrator breaks a goal into subtasks, hands them to worker agents with different tools or prompts, and merges the results.
eras.built: Agent teams for research, code migration and analysis; orchestration frameworks.
eras.broke: Coordination overhead grows fast, and someone still has to check every worker’s output.

eras.name: Agent swarms with verifiers
eras.short: Hundreds to thousands of agents work against an automatic checker that accepts only correct results.
eras.how: Instead of trusting agents, you trust the verifier: a proof checker, test suite or simulator. Agents propose, the verifier filters, survivors get refined. Memory layers start letting agents keep what they learn.
eras.built: 1,000-agent formal proof of Fermat in ~30h; AI-designed quantum circuits beating human designs; Signal's crypto code verified by agents in Lean.
eras.broke: Still open: it only works where a strict automatic check exists.
eras.marks: Fermat formalization (9 Nov 2026), AI quantum circuits (10 Nov 2026), AlphaProof Code on Signal (10 Nov 2026)

eras.name: World models and continual learning
eras.short: Contenders for what comes next: models that learn physics from observation and keep learning after deployment.
eras.how: World models simulate how an environment will change when you act, which lets agents plan in the physical world. Continual learning updates the model from experience without retraining from scratch.
eras.built: Research prototypes, robotics simulation, NeurIPS 2026 workshops.
eras.broke: Not yet reliable outside labs. Watch Frontier for signals.
eras.marks: Genie, V-JEPA, Continual World Models workshop (NeurIPS 2026)

weeks.label: Week of 16 Nov 2026
shifts: GPT-6.2 Astra rated High for self-improvement; OpenAI agents finish 46% of 2–4 hour research tasks; models now redesign chips for OpenAI and AMD.
Five big US banks put third-party agent losses on customers; Singapore's central bank warned agents could speed up deposit flight.
Azure gates agent writes with per-agent Entra IDs and Microsoft's Copilot Autopilot ships with its own identity and memory.
Reuters reported Meta's Muse read Signal messages through OS permissions; Apple responded with agent-specific prompts.
Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, Nvidia posted $115.8B revenue and Isomorphic raised $5B.

weeks.label: Week of 9 Nov 2026
shifts: Fermat formalization, AI-designed quantum circuits, Google's Lean-verified quantum programs and AlphaProof Code all paired many agents with a strict checker.
DeepMind verified Signal's one-to-one crypto down to machine instructions in about four weeks.
IBM's LLMON and Gemini 4 Hydrogen both led with prompt-injection resilience.
New York opened RAISE Act registration; Japan weighs binding orders; nonprofits sued to halt frontier development.
CEO resigned 12 Nov with Kress as interim; Nvidia earnings on 17 Nov and Anthropic IPO pricing on 18 Nov follow.

weeks.label: Week of 2 Nov 2026
shifts: Anthropic’s S-1/A describes Claude Code as an agent that plans, writes, tests and debugs; Antigravity 2.0 ships a standalone agent manager.
Agility begins trading on Nasdaq as AGLT.
IBM Nighthawk anchors a new algorithm center in Chicago, beside a GPU error-correction testbed.
After the midterms, lawmakers prepare bills on model testing and liability.
